query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior under high temperature loading emerges from localized strain concentrations at straight grain boundaries that trigger rapid intergranular crack initiation. Conversely, inducing serrated grain boundaries through a controlled slow cooling process promotes local ordering interactions with coarsened γ′ precipitates, which homogenize strain distribution and delay brittle failure.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, compositionally complex HEA with an FCC matrix containing fine γ′ precipitates and predominantly straight grain boundaries achieved via rapid cooling after solution heat treatment.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the cooling rate during the solution heat treatment to produce alloys with controlled grain-boundary morphologies ranging from straight (rapid cooling) to serrated (slow cooling).
generation.conditions: Service-relevant mechanical loading conditions at elevated temperatures (e.g., tensile and creep tests at approximately 650°C) under variable strain rate protocols.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary morphology, specifically the transition from straight to serrated boundaries mediated by interactions with coarsened γ′ precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Straight grain boundaries lead to high local strain concentrations at triple junctions, promoting vacancy coalescence and intergranular crack propagation under load. Serrated grain boundaries, formed through slow cooling that allows γ′ precipitate coarsening, redistribute local strains more evenly, delaying crack initiation and propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples produced with serrated grain boundaries will exhibit significantly improved high-temperature tensile fracture strain and extended creep rupture life compared to samples with straight grain boundaries. Additionally, measurements will reveal a marked reduction (approximately >50% decrease) in local strain concentration at grain-boundary triple junctions in the serrated samples.
generation.baseline: HEA samples with straight grain boundaries produced by rapid cooling after solution heat treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under service-relevant high-temperature conditions (around 650°C) and under both tensile and creep loading regimes; its validity for other temperatures or loading modalities remains to be determined.
generation.uncertainty: While the reduction in strain localization with serrated boundaries is expected to mitigate brittle behavior, the precise contribution of any stress-induced local ordering versus simple geometric effects of the serrations, as well as potential interactions with varying γ′ precipitate sizes, remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HEA samples with identical compositions. Process one group using rapid cooling after solution heat treatment to obtain predominantly straight grain boundaries, and process the other group using a controlled slow cooling rate to induce serrated grain boundaries. Subject both groups to high-temperature tensile and creep tests at ~650°C. Use high-resolution electron microscopy and strain-mapping techniques (such as EBSD-based kernel average misorientation analysis) to quantify grain-boundary morphology and local strain concentrations.
measurements: Grain-boundary morphology (quantified by wavelength and amplitude of serrations)
Local strain concentration at grain-boundary triple junctions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA samples with induced serrated grain boundaries do not show significantly improved tensile ductility and extended creep life, or if local strain concentrations at the grain boundaries are not statistically lower than in the straight boundary samples, then the hypothesis—that serrated grain boundaries mitigate brittle behavior via reduced strain localization—will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. For both HT-1 and HT-2 samples, microstructures contained a mixture of equiaxed grains (Figure 5(a,b)), and according to the KAM analysis, internal strains of the as-prepared sample were relieved (Figure 5(c,d)). However, when testing temperature was increased to 650°C, a significant hot ductility drop was observed for HT-1 sample. According to Figure 7(b), the facet cleavage surface and the limited amount of plastic deformation indicate that the failure mechanism was brittle intergranular fracture. The brittleness of HT-1 sample was even more pronounced under creep at 650°C as the creep fracture strain was only 0.03%. Cleavage edges on crept fracture surface (Figure 9(b)) and crack propagation along straight grain boundary (Figure 10(b)) indicate the vulnerability of straight grain boundary in HT-1 samples at elevated temperature. According to the local strain concentration at triple junctions of grain boundaries (Figure 11(a)), it is probable that HT-1 samples encountered an embrittlement at 650°C. The effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties has been investigated for a high-entropy alloy (Al8Co35Cr18Ni34Ti3Nb2Zr0.005B0.01 (at.%)) fabricated by selective laser melting, the followings are findings of this work: Serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. The inferior ductility of straight grain boundary at 650°C was attributed to the grain boundary embrittlement caused by strain concentration at triple junctions and fast intergranular crack propagation. The slow cooling process of the post heat treatment could coarsen the γ′ particles and encourage interactions with mobile grain boundaries to from serrated grain boundaries. Analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. Serrated grain boundaries could reduce local strain concentration and provide resistance against intergranular cracking.

decision.trend: Early HEA research was directed at achieving the best strength–ductility balance by designing multi‐phase or lamellar microstructures (PMC4145285, PMC6353877) and by understanding dislocation dynamics in complex lattices (PMC4949441, PMC7311485, PMC8446014). Recent studies such as PMC9848264 have shown that even in high-entropy alloys—which avoid the conventional grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation—the morphology of the grain boundaries (e.g., straight versus serrated) critically influences ductility and toughness under high-temperature loading. This work demonstrated that altering cooling rates to modulate grain-boundary geometry can mitigate hot ductility drops via more homogeneous strain distributions. However, while these approaches improve ductility in engineered samples, the fundamental mechanism driving a transition to brittle behavior in an inherent single-phase HEA, under service-like conditions, remains unclear.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved how (or if) intrinsic microstructural instabilities, such as local atomic-scale chemical fluctuations or stress-induced ordering at grain boundaries under service loading conditions, could trigger a brittle transition in an otherwise single-phase high-entropy alloy. In other words, a clear, testable mechanistic link must be established to distinguish an emergent brittle behavior driven by dynamic grain-boundary phenomena or local ordering from conventional segregation- or precipitation-induced embrittlement.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the cooling rate during solution heat treatment to produce a series of alloys with quantitatively controlled grain-boundary morphologies (from near‐planar to increasingly serrated) and compare their fracture behavior under service-relevant mechanical loading (including variable strain rate and temperature cycling tests).
decision.why: This approach builds directly on the trend observed in studies like PMC9848264, where modifying grain-boundary morphology profoundly affected ductility. By using controlled-variable experiments to create a continuous microstructural lever (grain-boundary shape), researchers can test the hypothesis that subtle, service-induced local ordering or instability at the grain boundaries (absent conventional segregation) is responsible for brittle behavior. The controlled comparison against a baseline single-phase HEA (with less serrated boundaries) under identical testing conditions provides a decisive means to validate or falsify the mechanistic hypothesis.
